overview: Heterodontosaurus tucki was a small, early ornithischian from the Early Jurassic of South Africa (~200–190 Ma), about 1.2 metres long, named for its three different tooth types — a unique feature among dinosaurs. It had large canine-like tusks, small incisiform teeth at the jaw front, and cheek teeth with leaf-shaped crowns for processing vegetation, resembling the dental diversity of heterodont mammals.

As one of the earliest well-documented ornithischians, Heterodontosaurus provides crucial information about the ancestral ornithischian body plan. Its small size, complex dentition and possible semi-bipedal locomotion represent a generalised early ornithischian that preceded the major radiations of the group into stegosaurs, ankylosaurs, ornithopods and ceratopsians.

articles.title: Discovery and the three-tooth system
articles.body: Alfred Crompton and Alan Charig described Heterodontosaurus tucki in 1962. The remarkable skull preserves three distinct tooth types (heterodonty): small incisiform premaxillary teeth for cropping, large caniniform teeth (tusks) in both upper and lower jaws, and leaf-shaped cheek teeth for chewing. This combination is unique in dinosaurs; the tusks may have been used in display or intraspecific combat.

articles.title: Anatomy and posture
articles.body: Heterodontosaurus had long forelimbs relative to its body — more so than most ornithopods — suggesting some use of the forelimbs in foraging. The hindlimbs show classic bipedal proportions. A well-preserved skeleton at the South African Museum shows remarkable preservation of the skull and most postcranial elements, allowing detailed study of early ornithischian anatomy.

articles.title: Early ornithischian radiation
articles.body: The Elliot Formation yields several other early dinosaurs (prosauropods, small theropods) alongside Heterodontosaurus, providing a snapshot of an Early Jurassic South African community. As a very early ornithischian, Heterodontosaurus shows the clade before it diversified into its major subgroups — its relatively unspecialised body plan and diverse dentition may reflect the ancestral ornithischian condition.

record.description: Heterodontosaurus tucki was a small bipedal ornithischian from the upper Elliot Formation of South Africa. Several skulls and one nearly complete skeleton document a compact herbivore with a beak, cheek teeth and enlarged canine-like teeth.
facts: The profile Late Triassic age is incorrect; secure material is Early Jurassic.
Canine-like teeth do not prove a carnivorous diet and may have had display or defence roles.
Jaw mechanics and tooth wear support effective plant processing, while opportunistic animal matter remains possible but unproven.

presentation.heroLead: A small, fast-moving plant-eater from Early Jurassic South Africa whose three kinds of teeth, including enlarged canine-like tusks, make it one of the best-understood early ornithischians.

animalParagraphs: Heterodontosaurus was a turkey-sized ornithischian that walked on two legs, with a short skull, a horny beak at the tip of the jaws and a long tail. The most complete individual is a little over a metre long; published mass estimates fall in the range of a few kilograms, and the animal was among the smallest dinosaurs of the Elliot fauna.

Its name refers to its unusual dentition. Small teeth at the front of the upper jaw were followed by a pair of enlarged, canine-like tusks in both jaws, then a row of tightly packed cheek teeth with chisel-shaped crowns. Wear surfaces on the cheek teeth and the jaw joint indicate that the upper and lower tooth rows slid against one another to grind plant food, one of the earliest examples of true chewing in dinosaurs.

The hands were relatively large, with five fingers and strong claws on the first three, and the forelimb bones show muscle attachments that suggest a grasping or digging capacity. The hindlimb was long and lightly built, with the shin bones and upper foot bones fused together in the near-complete skeleton, a feature more often associated with fast runners.
animalHighlights: Three distinct tooth types: small front teeth, enlarged canine-like tusks and closely packed cheek teeth.
Tooth wear and jaw anatomy show that the cheek teeth ground against one another, an early form of chewing.
Fused shin and ankle bones and a long, lightly built hindlimb are consistent with an agile two-legged runner.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.level: Supported by tooth wear and jaw mechanics
lifeCards.reason: Grinding wear on the cheek teeth and the beak support a plant diet. The tusks do not establish meat-eating; opportunistic animal food remains possible but unproven.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Long hindlimbs, fused lower-leg and ankle bones and short forelimbs indicate habitual two-legged movement; running speed is not directly measured.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: SAM-PK-K1332 and AM 4766 are near-complete adults or near-adults, so length is measured rather than extrapolated. Mass is an estimate.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: No skin or filament impressions are preserved for Heterodontosaurus itself; bristle-like structures in restorations come from the related Tianyulong.

presentation.classificationSummary: Heterodontosaurus is the name-giving member of Heterodontosauridae, a family of small, early-diverging ornithischians. Most analyses place heterodontosaurids near the base of the ornithischian tree, but whether they sit closer to the marginocephalians or outside all other ornithischians remains debated.

Compare with an Early Jurassic armoured ornithischian of similar size from North America.
Compare with a beaked, self-sharpening-toothed ornithischian sometimes linked to heterodontosaurids through the marginocephalian hypothesis.

questions.title: What were the tusks for?
questions.copy: The enlarged canine-like teeth have been read as display, defence or feeding structures. They occur in the smallest known juvenile, which weakens a purely sex-linked explanation, but no single function is established.

questions.title: Did it eat anything other than plants?
questions.copy: The cheek teeth are clearly built for grinding vegetation. Whether Heterodontosaurus also took insects or small animals, as some authors have proposed, cannot be tested from the fossils.

questions.title: Where do heterodontosaurids belong?
questions.copy: Heterodontosaurids have been placed as the earliest branch of Ornithischia and, alternatively, close to pachycephalosaurs and ceratopsians. The answer changes with the dataset used.

panel.headline: Complete skulls and two near-complete articulated skeletons.
panel.standfirst: Heterodontosaurus is known from a well-preserved holotype skull, a near-complete articulated skeleton with skull, a second near-complete skeleton studied by synchrotron scanning, and several further skulls and partial specimens, including a very small juvenile.

coverage.label: Excellent
coverage.basis: Every skeletal region is represented, most of it in articulated skeletons from more than one individual. Only the tip of the tail and soft tissues are missing.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: The skull is known in detail from the holotype and several other individuals. The near-complete skeleton SAM-PK-K1332 preserves the neck, back, sacrum and most of the tail, both girdles and all four limbs in articulation, and AM 4766 adds a second articulated skeleton that includes rarely preserved sternal ribs and gastralia.
knownRemains.note: The end of the tail is not preserved in any specimen, and no skin, filament or gut-content evidence is known for the genus itself.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: Several complete or near-complete skulls with lower jaws, including the holotype, the skull of SAM-PK-K1332 and the partial juvenile skull SAM-PK-K10487, preserving the beak, tusks and cheek teeth.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Articulated cervical, dorsal, sacral and caudal series in SAM-PK-K1332 and AM 4766, with ribs, gastralia and sternal ribs; the tip of the tail is missing.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Shoulder and pelvic girdles and complete forelimbs and hindlimbs, including articulated hands and feet with fused lower-leg and ankle elements.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: Articulated skeletons in fine-grained rock, studied by synchrotron scanning; tooth enamel microstructure and histology sampled. No skin or filament impressions.

specimenCards.title: SAM-PK-K1332 and AM 4766
specimenCards.description: SAM-PK-K1332 is an articulated skull and skeleton described in 1976 that fixed the body proportions of the genus. AM 4766, in the Albany Museum, is a second near-complete skeleton whose synchrotron scans in 2021 revealed gastralia and mobile sternal ribs.
specimenCards.meta: Voyizane, Krommespruit mountain and Eastern Cape · upper Elliot and Clarens formations

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: Skulls with complete dentitions, tooth-wear facets, and two articulated skeletons preserving vertebral column, girdles, limbs, gastralia and sternal ribs.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: The wear facets and jaw joint record grinding of plant food; the limb proportions and fused ankle indicate an agile biped; the sternal ribs and gastralia have been used to model an early form of ventilation.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: The function of the tusks, the full breadth of the diet, whether the body carried filaments as in Tianyulong, colour, and the exact position of heterodontosaurids within Ornithischia.
